_how_to_edit: The story page, replay map and home hero read this file on every load. Edit it, run `node groundstop/src/build.js`, commit and push to main; no Squarespace edit is needed. Times are hours on an Eastern clock on Nov. 13, 2026 (17.5 = 5:30 p.m.; values past 24 mean Nov. 14). Set lift to null while the stop is in effect.
headline_status: The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, after 4 hours and 21 minutes
cause: Overloaded routers on older FAA hardware
moments: A Friday afternoon, with flights departing on schedule across the country.
About 3:10 p.m.
Flights bound for Chicago O’Hare are stopped over communications problems, and Midway follows three minutes later.
Radar and communications at centers and approach facilities across the country become unstable, the transportation secretary says later.
Nationwide ground stop. More than 3,100 flights already in the air are allowed to continue to their destinations.
The transportation secretary says a communication issue is affecting air route traffic control centers.
The FAA advisory now runs to 11:30 p.m. Eastern, and no end time is confirmed.
About 5:15 p.m.
The FAA says a temporary telecommunications outage caused the stop, and officials say they see no sign of an attack.
About 6:00 p.m.
The FAA says the stop remains in effect and that flights will be released as each en route center recovers.
Fox Weather counts 598 commercial flights still in the air, down from more than 3,100 when the stop began.
About 7:10 p.m.
An airline source tells CNN that major airlines could shut down operations for the rest of the night.
FlightAware counts 5,117 cancellations and 9,814 delays, and JetBlue and United call off most of their remaining Friday flights.
The airspace reopens, the transportation secretary says, about 4 hours and 21 minutes after the nationwide stop began.
By 8:48 p.m.
At a White House briefing, the transportation secretary says older hardware failed and that none of the FAA’s new systems went down.
facts: Eastern start time, the only one of the three stops to begin after noon
flights in the air when the stop began, allowed to finish their trips
length of the stop, against about 90 minutes in 2023
unknown: What is not known. Officials blame overloaded routers on older FAA hardware but have not said what overloaded them or where the failure began. Duffy said SMART, the AI rerouting tool expanded on Nov. 10, is not connected to the equipment that failed.
status_html: The FAA lifted the stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, 4 hours and 21 minutes after it began, and the airspace was operating normally by 7:30 a.m. Saturday, according to CBS News. Airlines were still catching up on Saturday: FlightAware counted more than 9,100 canceled U.S. flights on Friday, about seven times the 1,300-plus canceled on the day of the 2023 stop, and CBS News, citing FlightAware, reported more than 3,800 Saturday cancellations and about 2,000 Saturday delays at 10:36 a.m. Eastern.
compare_html: Friday’s stop lasted 261 minutes, close to three times the roughly 90 minutes of 2023, and it began late on a Friday afternoon where the 2023 stop began early on a Wednesday, which left airlines almost none of the day to recover. The data firm Cirium said more than 15% of the 26,284 flights scheduled to depart the United States on Friday were canceled or never took off.
notknown_html:
Officials have not named the technology that overloaded the routers, said where the failure began or explained why it reached all 22 centers, and Duffy said on Friday night that the FAA was still working out the details. CBS News reported that an update to the network, which the contractor L3Harris operates, made the system reboot, and the FAA has not confirmed that account.

Officials say they have found no sign of a cyberattack. SMART, the AI rerouting tool the FAA expanded to all 22 centers on Nov. 10, is not connected to the equipment that failed, according to Duffy, and its contractor said the stop was not a result of the tool. Reports of Friday’s delays range from 7,068 to more than 24,500, so this page gives no final delay count. This story reflects what was known at 11:02 a.m. Eastern on Nov. 14, 2026.
cause_html: Most likely cause: switches and routers on the FAA’s decades-old telecommunications network were overloaded with data and began returning inconsistent readings at 3:36 p.m. Eastern, 18 minutes before the stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. Administration officials told the Associated Press that new technology being added to the system overloaded the older equipment. The FAA has not published a final finding.
